notes.h: Climatic environments and how they are classified
notes.b: A climatic environment is a large area with a similar pattern of temperature, precipitation and seasons, usually matched by similar vegetation and soils. Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere; climate is the average pattern over many years (see the note Weather maps and weather data).
points: The Köppen system, devised by Wladimir Köppen, a German-Russian climatologist, divides the world mainly by temperature and precipitation thresholds that match vegetation.
Its broad groups are tropical, dry, warm temperate, cool temperate (continental) and polar.
Climates are arranged in belts by latitude, then modified by distance from the sea, ocean currents, relief, and whether a place lies on the east or the west side of a continent.

Controls on climate: latitude and insolation; pressure belts and planetary winds with their seasonal shift; air masses; ocean currents; continentality; altitude and relief (explained in the notes Solar energy and its redistribution and Atmospheric and oceanic circulation).
Diagram: a world map of the main climate regions.

notes.b: The equatorial (tropical rainforest) climate lies close to the equator, mainly in the Amazon Basin, the Congo Basin and South-East Asia (Indonesia and Malaysia).
points: Temperatures are high all year, with monthly means of about 26–28 °C.
The annual range is tiny, about 2–3 °C, but the daily range is larger than the annual range: afternoon highs of about 30–32 °C and night lows of about 22–24 °C.
The sun is always high in the sky and is overhead at the equator at the equinoxes (March and September), so there is little change in heat input through the year.
Cloud cover stops temperatures rising much above the low 30s °C.
Pressure is permanently low in the equatorial trough (the ITCZ, or doldrums), where the trade winds converge; winds are light and variable.

notes.h: Equatorial climate: precipitation, humidity and the daily weather cycle
points: Rainfall is over 2,000 mm a year (Manaus, Brazil, about 2,300 mm) and falls in every month.
There are often two wetter peaks after the equinoxes, when the overhead sun and the ITCZ pass over.
The rain is convectional: intense heating and very moist air from warm seas and forest transpiration build towering clouds that produce heavy afternoon thunderstorms.
Trade winds converge at the ITCZ, which lifts and reinforces the moist air.
Relative humidity is often over 80%, and the air is humid at night too.
Daily cycle: a clear, calm, humid morning; cumulus building by late morning; cumulonimbus and torrential rain with thunder in the afternoon; clearing in the evening.
The climate has no temperate-style seasons.

notes.h: Equatorial climate: vegetation and human response
points: Tropical rainforest grows on latosols; the note One major biome in detail gives the detail.
Forest clearance for farming and timber is the main human pressure on the rainforest.

notes.h: Monsoon climate: location, definition and seasons
notes.b: A monsoon climate has a seasonal reversal of wind direction, bringing a very wet summer and a dry winter. The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word for season. The classic monsoon climate is in South and South-East Asia, especially India; weaker monsoon climates occur in other tropical regions.
points: The hot season before the rains: temperatures often exceed 40 °C on the northern plains.
The wet south-west monsoon, from June to September: slightly cooler than the hot season because of cloud and rain.
The cool dry season: pleasant, with cool nights in the north.
The south-west monsoon normally reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers all of India by mid-July.

notes.h: Monsoon climate: how the summer monsoon forms
points: 1. Intense heating of the land and of the high land to the north creates low pressure over north-west India.
2. The ITCZ moves north.
3. The south-east trade winds cross the equator and are deflected by the Coriolis force into south-west winds, which gather moisture over the sea to the south.
4. The subtropical jet stream shifts north of the mountains to the north, allowing the monsoon to burst suddenly.
Reference: the note India explains the monsoon in more detail.

notes.h: Monsoon climate: rainfall pattern and the winter monsoon
points: Relief rain falls on the Western Ghats and on the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya; Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, in the Khasi Hills, are among the wettest places on earth.
The Deccan lies in a rain shadow, and rainfall decreases towards the north-west, with the Thar Desert in Rajasthan the driest region.
Kolkata is wetter than Delhi.
In winter the land cools and high pressure builds over the interior of Asia; dry north-east winds blow off the land.
Mountains to the north block cold air from the interior of Asia from reaching India.
The east coast of southern India gets winter rain from the north-east monsoon after it has crossed the sea.

notes.h: Monsoon climate: variability, hazards and human response
points: Late, weak or broken monsoons bring drought; very heavy ones bring floods.
The Odisha super cyclone of October 1999 killed about 10,000 people.
El Niño years often bring a weaker Indian monsoon (see El Niño below).
Kharif crops such as rice are sown with the monsoon rains; rabi crops such as wheat rely on stored water and irrigation.

notes.h: Cool temperate oceanic (mid-latitude west coast) climate: location and temperature
notes.b: This climate lies on west coasts in the path of the westerlies, including north-west Europe: Ireland, Britain, north-west France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and coastal Norway. Other west coasts in the same latitude belt in both hemispheres share it.
points: Winters are mild and summers are cool, with a small annual range: Ireland's mean January is about 4–7 °C and its mean July about 14–16 °C, an annual range of about 10 °C.
Frost and snow are infrequent on low ground.
The climate of Ireland is described at Core level in the note Physical regions.

notes.h: Cool temperate oceanic climate: precipitation and weather
points: Rain falls in all months, with a maximum in autumn and winter and many wet days: about 150 a year in the east and south-east of Ireland and up to about 225 in parts of the west.
Annual rainfall is about 750 mm in the driest east (around Dublin), about 1,000–1,250 mm across much of the west, and over 2,000 mm on many western mountains.
Most rain is frontal (cyclonic), with relief rain on west-facing mountains; amounts fall from west to east.
Prevailing south-westerly winds bring maritime air off the Atlantic.
The North Atlantic Drift, the extension of the Gulf Stream, warms winter air and seas.
The sea heats and cools slowly, moderating the seasons.
Depressions form frequently on the polar front and are steered by the jet stream, so the weather is changeable as depressions and ridges of high pressure alternate.
Occasional anticyclones bring dry spells, most often in summer.
Tropical and polar maritime air masses are the most common.
Vegetation is deciduous woodland and grass on brown earths.
Eastwards the oceanic influence weakens, and the climate grades into the continental climate of central and eastern Europe (see the note Physical regions).

notes.b: The Mediterranean climate lies on the west sides of continents: the Mediterranean Basin, central and southern California, central Chile, the Cape Town area of South Africa, and south-western and southern Australia (around Perth and Adelaide).
points: Summers are hot: lowland July means are about 25 °C or more, for example in southern Italy.
Winters are mild: coastal January means are about 9–12 °C, and frost is rare on the coasts.
Inland and upland areas have hotter summers and colder winters than the coast.
Rainfall is moderate, under 600 mm a year on parts of the Puglia lowlands and Sicily, and most of it falls from October to March.
Summers are dry, with drought for several months; rain often falls in intense downpours that cause flash floods and soil erosion.
In summer the subtropical high pressure belt moves poleward over the region, bringing sinking, warming air, clear skies and no rain.
In winter the pressure belts shift towards the equator, so the westerlies and their depressions bring rain; the warm Mediterranean Sea also spawns its own winter depressions.
On some of these coasts cold currents (the California, Humboldt, Benguela and Canary currents) keep summers cooler and drier.
The sirocco is a hot, dry, dusty wind from the Sahara; the mistral and the bora are cold winds (see Atmospheric and oceanic circulation).

notes.h: Mediterranean climate: vegetation, hazards and human response
points: Drought-tolerant vegetation: olives, vines and cork oak, and maquis scrub; citrus grows where it is irrigated.
Hazards: summer water shortage, and wildfires in hot, dry, windy summers.
The Mati wildfire near Athens, Greece, in July 2018 killed about 100 people, one of the deadliest wildfires in Europe.
Human response: water storage and irrigation, and tourism (see Climate and economic development).

notes.b: The continental climate lies in the interiors of the large northern-hemisphere continents, far from the sea: across central and eastern Europe and Russia (Moscow), the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia, the Canadian Prairies and the Great Plains of the USA. There is no large equivalent in the southern hemisphere, which has too little land at these latitudes.
points: Winters are very cold, with monthly means well below 0 °C for several months: Moscow about −7 °C in January and Winnipeg about −16 °C in January.
Summers are warm to hot: Moscow about 19 °C and Winnipeg about 20 °C in July.
The annual range is large and increases with distance from the sea; Verkhoyansk has an annual range of over 60 °C.
Spring and autumn are short.
Precipitation is low to moderate and decreases into the interior: Moscow receives about 600–700 mm a year, with a summer maximum.
The summer maximum comes from convectional thunderstorms as the land heats up; winter precipitation falls as snow, which lies for months.
Continentality: the land heats and cools quickly, and there is no sea to moderate the temperature.
Distance from the oceans: the westerlies have lost most of their moisture crossing the land, and mountains block Pacific air from reaching the interior.
The winter Siberian High, a cold, dry, clear thermal anticyclone, sits over the continent; North America has an equivalent.
Summer low pressure over the heated land draws in some moist air.

notes.h: Continental climate: extremes, vegetation and human response
points: Hazards: blizzards; cold waves of arctic air; summer heatwaves, drought and dust storms, as in the Dust Bowl of the 1930s on the Great Plains (see Human interaction: mass movement); floods when the spring snowmelt comes.

Vegetation is temperate grassland (steppe and prairie) on chernozems, the black soils of the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia, the Prairies and the Pampas (see Soil processes and the global pattern of soils).
Human response: wheat and maize belts on the grassland; boreal forest further north.

notes.b: Hot deserts lie on the west sides of continents, for example the Sahara, the Atacama and the Namib (see One major biome in detail).
points: Rainfall is very low and unreliable because of sinking air in the subtropical high pressure belt, offshore trade winds, cold currents and rain shadows.
The highest air temperatures on earth were recorded: 56.7 °C at Furnace Creek, Death Valley, on 10 July 1913, a WMO record.
The daily range is very large, often 20–30 °C or more, because dry, cloudless air lets heat escape at night.
Fog forms on coasts with cold currents.
The Sahara covers about 9 million km², the world's largest hot desert; the Atacama is the driest non-polar desert.
Cold currents on desert coasts: the Canary (Sahara), Benguela (Namib), Humboldt (Atacama) and California (Sonoran coast).
From equator to pole: temperature falls and seasonal contrasts grow with latitude.
From coast to interior: continentality increases the annual range; Ireland's annual range is about 10 °C, while Verkhoyansk's is over 60 °C.
From west to east coasts: cold currents cool and dry west coasts, while warm currents such as the North Atlantic Drift warm them.
With altitude: temperature falls with height, so high mountains have a vertical sequence of climates, and snow lies on high ground even near the equator.
Across a mountain range: the windward side gets relief rain, while the leeward side lies in a rain shadow, as the Deccan does in India.
Climate boundaries are transition zones that shift: the Sahel lies between the desert and wetter land and moves with the ITCZ from year to year, with rainfall of roughly 200–600 mm.

notes.h: Causes of climate change over time
points: Timescales: long-term change over millions of years (plate movement, mountain building); glacial cycles over tens to hundreds of thousands of years; centuries (the Little Ice Age); years (El Niño and volcanic eruptions); and recent human-caused warming.
Milankovitch orbital cycles (see Ice Ages below).
Changes in solar output.

Volcanic eruptions: sulphate aerosols reflect sunlight and cool the earth for a year or two; after Mount Pinatubo, Philippines, erupted in June 1991, global average temperature fell by about 0.5 °C for about a year (1992).
Plate tectonics: moving continents and opening or closing seaways change ocean currents.
Changes in ocean circulation.
Feedbacks: the ice–albedo feedback, and CO2 and methane released or absorbed by oceans and permafrost.

The enhanced greenhouse effect from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture; land-use change and aerosols also alter the climate. The sources of each gas are in the note Environmental pollution.
Ice cores: bubbles of ancient air record past CO2, and oxygen isotopes record past temperature; Antarctic ice cores (EPICA Dome C) record about 800,000 years of climate and CO2.
Ocean-floor sediments.
Tree rings.
Pollen preserved in peat bogs and lake muds; Irish bogs record changes in vegetation, and therefore climate, since the Ice Age.
Glacial landforms (see Glacial processes, patterns and associated landforms).
Historical records such as harvest dates, frost fairs and ships' logs; instrument records since the 19th century.
The Quaternary glaciation began about 2.6 million years ago; since then the earth has swung between long glacial periods and shorter, warm interglacials.
Over the last 800,000 years the cycle has been about 100,000 years long; we now live in an interglacial.
At the Last Glacial Maximum, about 20,000 years ago, ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe, including Ireland.
Global sea level was about 120 m lower than today, exposing land bridges between islands and continents.
Global average temperature was several degrees colder, and the climate belts were pushed towards the equator.

notes.h: Ice Ages: Ireland and the effects of glaciation
points: Ireland had two main cold stages, the Munsterian and the Midlandian. The Munsterian ice covered almost all of Ireland; the Midlandian ice had gone by about 10,000 years ago.
The evidence is in the landscape of drumlins, eskers, corries and U-shaped valleys (see Glacial processes, patterns and associated landforms).
Isostatic rebound and raised beaches are after-effects of the ice (see Isostasy).

Effects beyond the ice: drier, windier climates; deserts expanded; loess was blown from outwash plains; sea level fell; plants and animals migrated towards the equator and recolonised the land afterwards.

Milankovitch cycles, named after Milutin Milanković, a Serbian scientist who calculated them in the early 20th century, change the distribution of sunlight by latitude and season more than its total amount.

Eccentricity (the shape of the orbit) varies over about 100,000 years; obliquity (the tilt, varying between about 22° and 24.5°) over about 41,000 years; precession (the wobble of the axis) over roughly 19,000–26,000 years.
When northern summers are cool, snow survives the winter and ice sheets grow.
Feedbacks amplify the small orbital change: more ice raises albedo, and colder oceans absorb more CO2, lowering greenhouse gases.
Ice cores show CO2 near 180 ppm at glacial maxima and about 280 ppm in interglacials.
Changes in the Atlantic circulation.
Land near the North Pole allows ice sheets to build.

notes.h: Shorter cold and warm periods in historical times
points: Medieval Warm Period, roughly AD 950–1250: a regional warm phase mainly in the North Atlantic and Europe. Vines were grown further north in England than in the colder centuries that followed.
Norse settlers led by Erik the Red settled Greenland from about AD 985; the settlements were abandoned in the 15th century as the climate cooled.
Little Ice Age, roughly the 14th to the mid-19th century, coldest in the 17th century: a regional cold phase mainly in the North Atlantic and Europe, with Alpine glaciers advancing.
The River Thames in London froze in severe winters, and frost fairs were held on the ice, the last in 1814.
The Maunder Minimum (about 1645–1715), a period with very few sunspots, coincided with some of the coldest decades.
In Ireland the Great Frost of the winter of 1739–40 was followed by famine in 1740–41.
The eruption of Tambora, Indonesia, in April 1815 led to 1816 being the year without a summer, with harvest failures across Europe and north-eastern North America.
CO2 was about 280 ppm before the Industrial Revolution and is over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s; it has been measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1958.
Global average surface temperature has risen about 1.1–1.2 °C since the late 1800s (IPCC).
2024 was the warmest year on record and the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels (Copernicus).
Arctic summer sea ice has shrunk by about 13% per decade since satellite records began in 1979.
Global sea level rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018 (IPCC).
Glaciers are retreating in most mountain regions.
Ireland's average temperature has risen about 0.9 °C since 1900 (EPA and Met Éireann).
The enhanced greenhouse effect: more CO2, methane and nitrous oxide absorb more outgoing long-wave radiation, so the heat budget is out of balance and the earth warms until a new balance is reached.
Most of the extra heat goes into the ocean.
Ice–albedo feedback: melting ice exposes dark ocean, which absorbs more heat; this is why the Arctic is warming fastest.
Water vapour feedback: warmer air holds more water vapour, itself a greenhouse gas.
Permafrost thaw releases methane and CO2.
Reduced ocean CO2 uptake as the water warms.

notes.h: Global warming: effects on climate patterns
points: A more intense hydrological cycle: heavier downpours and more severe droughts.
More intense heatwaves: the European heatwave of summer 2003 caused an estimated 70,000 or so extra deaths.
A poleward shift of climate belts and storm tracks, and an expansion of the subtropical dry zones.
A possible weakening of the Atlantic circulation (AMOC) (see Atmospheric and oceanic circulation).
Stronger tropical cyclones.
Sea-level rise from the thermal expansion of warmer water and the melting of land ice.

notes.h: Global warming: effects on Ireland and responses
points: Ireland: warmer temperatures; wetter winters and more flooding; a risk of summer drought, as in the summer of 2018; stronger storms and coastal erosion (see Environmental pollution).
The IPCC was set up in 1988; its Sixth Assessment Report (2021) stated that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land.
The Paris Agreement of 2015 aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue 1.5 °C; policy detail is in the note Environmental pollution.

notes.h: El Niño: normal conditions in the Pacific (Walker circulation)
points: Strong south-east trade winds push warm surface water westward across the Pacific, piling up a warm pool near Indonesia, where sea level is higher.

Warm, moist air rises over the warm pool, producing low pressure and heavy rain. Air returns eastward at height and sinks over the cool eastern Pacific, giving high pressure and dry conditions on the coast of Peru.
Cold, nutrient-rich water upwells off Peru (the Humboldt Current), supporting the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, the largest single-species fishery in the world.
The Walker circulation is named after Gilbert Walker, a British scientist who worked in India in the early 20th century.
Every 2–7 years the trade winds weaken or even reverse, and the warm water flows back east towards South America.
The thermocline deepens in the east and upwelling stops; sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific rise well above normal; the zone of rising air and rain shifts east.
El Niño is a natural variation; scientists are still researching whether global warming changes it.
Named by Peruvian fishermen. Together with the Southern Oscillation, the see-saw of air pressure across the Pacific, it is called ENSO.
Heavy rain and floods in coastal Peru and Ecuador, which are normally dry.
Collapse of the anchoveta catch and the fishmeal industry, with seabird deaths.
Drought in Indonesia and the Philippines, with crop failure and forest fires.
Often a weaker Indian monsoon.
Fewer Atlantic hurricanes and more in the central and eastern Pacific.
Global average temperature rises temporarily, and strong El Niño years set temperature records.
Effects on Ireland and Europe are weak and uncertain.
1972–73: an El Niño, combined with overfishing, caused the collapse of the Peruvian anchoveta fishery.
1982–83 and 1997–98: very strong El Niños. In 1997–98 coastal Peru and Ecuador had severe floods, and drought in Indonesia allowed huge forest fires whose smoke haze spread across South-East Asia.
2015–16: one of the three strongest El Niños on record.
2023–24: helped make 2023 and 2024 the warmest years on record.
Stronger trade winds, a cooler than normal eastern Pacific and stronger upwelling.
Heavier rain in Indonesia and in Queensland, Australia, drought in Peru, and more Atlantic hurricanes.
The strong La Niña of 2010–11 brought record rain and floods to Queensland, Australia, including the Brisbane flood of January 2011.
It shows the atmosphere and ocean acting as one linked system (see The atmosphere and oceans as linked systems).
It shows how a change in ocean circulation changes weather around the world (teleconnections).
Monitoring by buoys and satellites in the equatorial Pacific gives months of warning.

keyTerms.definition: A large area with a similar pattern of temperature, precipitation and seasons, usually matched by similar vegetation and soils.
A system that divides the world's climates mainly by temperature and precipitation thresholds that match vegetation.
A climate with a seasonal reversal of wind direction, bringing a very wet summer and a dry winter.
The Intertropical Convergence Zone, the belt near the equator where the trade winds converge and moist air rises.
The increase in temperature range and dryness with distance from the sea, because land heats and cools quickly.
A belt of high pressure and sinking air that moves seasonally, bringing dry conditions to the regions it covers.
Regular changes in the earth's orbit and axis that alter how sunlight is distributed by latitude and season, driving glacial cycles.
The process by which melting ice exposes darker surfaces that absorb more heat, causing further warming.
The warming of the central and eastern Pacific, with weakened trade winds, that disrupts weather around the world.
The opposite phase of ENSO, with stronger trade winds and a cooler than normal eastern Pacific.

factCards.term: Equatorial climate: location and temperature, with reasons
factCards.definition: The Amazon Basin, Congo Basin and South-East Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia). Monthly means about 26–28 °C, annual range only about 2–3 °C, because the sun is always high and overhead at the equinoxes; cloud stops maxima rising much above the low 30s °C.

factCards.term: Equatorial climate: rainfall amount, timing and causes
factCards.definition: Over 2,000 mm a year (Manaus, Brazil, about 2,300 mm), in every month, peaking after the equinoxes as the overhead sun and ITCZ pass. It is convectional: intense heating of very moist air, with the trade winds converging at the ITCZ in permanent low pressure.

factCards.term: Equatorial climate: the daily weather cycle
factCards.definition: A clear, calm, humid morning; cumulus building by late morning; cumulonimbus and torrential rain with thunder in the afternoon; clearing in the evening. Highs about 30–32 °C, night lows about 22–24 °C, so the daily range exceeds the annual range.

factCards.term: Indian monsoon climate: the three seasons
factCards.definition: The hot season (March–May), often over 40 °C on the northern plains before the rains; the wet south-west monsoon (June–September), slightly cooler under cloud and rain; the cool dry season (October–February), when dry north-east winds blow off the cooled land.

factCards.term: Summer monsoon over India: how it forms, in four steps
factCards.definition: Land heating creates low pressure over north-west India; the ITCZ moves north; south-east trades cross the equator and Coriolis turns them into moist south-west winds; the subtropical jet shifts north and the monsoon bursts, reaching Kerala around 1 June.

factCards.term: Indian monsoon: rainfall pattern with named places
factCards.definition: Relief rain on the Western Ghats (Konkan and Malabar coasts) and the Khasi Hills, where Mawsynram and Cherrapunji are among the wettest places on earth; the Deccan is in rain shadow; rain decreases north-west to the Thar Desert; Kolkata is wetter than Delhi.

factCards.term: Indian monsoon: hazards and human response
factCards.definition: Late, weak or broken monsoons bring drought, heavy ones floods; El Niño years often weaken the monsoon; the Odisha super cyclone of October 1999 killed about 10,000. Kharif crops such as rice are sown with the rains; rabi crops such as wheat need irrigation.

factCards.term: Cool temperate oceanic climate: location and temperature figures
factCards.definition: West coasts at about 40° to 60° in the westerlies: north-west Europe including Ireland, British Columbia and the US Pacific north-west, southern Chile, New Zealand, Tasmania. Ireland: January about 4–7 °C, July about 14–16 °C, annual range about 10 °C; frost and snow infrequent on low ground.

factCards.term: Cool temperate oceanic climate: five reasons for its character
factCards.definition: Prevailing south-westerlies bring maritime Atlantic air; the North Atlantic Drift warms winter air and seas; the sea heats and cools slowly; frequent depressions steered by the jet stream make weather changeable; occasional anticyclones give dry spells.

factCards.term: Mediterranean climate: where it is found
factCards.definition: On the west sides of continents: the Mediterranean Basin (e.g. southern Italy), central and southern California, central Chile, the Cape Town area of South Africa, and south-western and southern Australia around Perth and Adelaide.

factCards.term: Mediterranean climate: temperature and rainfall figures
factCards.definition: Lowland July means about 25 °C or more; coastal January about 9–12 °C, with frost rare. Most rain falls from October to March, under 600 mm a year on parts of the Puglia lowlands and Sicily; summers have months of drought, and downpours cause flash floods.

factCards.term: Mediterranean climate: why summers are dry and winters wet
factCards.definition: In summer the subtropical high moves poleward over the region, bringing sinking, warming air and clear skies. In winter the belts shift towards the equator, so westerly depressions bring rain; the warm Mediterranean Sea also spawns winter depressions.

factCards.term: Mediterranean climate: hazards and human response, with a named wildfire
factCards.definition: Summer water shortage; wildfires in hot, dry, windy summers, such as the Mati fire near Athens in July 2018, which killed about 100 people. Responses: drought-tolerant olives, vines, cork oak and maquis; irrigated citrus; water storage; tourism.

factCards.term: Continental climate: location and temperature figures
factCards.definition: Interiors of northern-hemisphere continents far from the sea: central and eastern Europe, Russia, the Canadian Prairies, the Great Plains. Moscow about −7 °C in January and 19 °C in July; Winnipeg about −16 °C and 20 °C. The range grows inland.

factCards.term: Continental climate: precipitation and its four causes
factCards.definition: Low to moderate (Moscow about 600–700 mm), with a summer maximum from convection and winter snow that lies for months. Causes: continentality; westerlies have lost moisture crossing the land; the cold, dry winter Siberian High; summer low pressure.

factCards.term: Continental climate: hazards and human response
factCards.definition: Blizzards and cold waves of arctic air; summer heatwaves, drought and dust storms, as in the Dust Bowl of the 1930s on the Great Plains; spring snowmelt floods. Temperate grassland on chernozems supports wheat and maize belts; boreal forest lies further north.

factCards.term: Hot desert climate: four characteristics and their reasons
factCards.definition: Little, unreliable rain (subtropical high, offshore trades, cold currents, rain shadow); the highest temperatures on earth (56.7 °C, Death Valley, 10 July 1913) under clear skies and a high sun; a daily range of 20–30 °C as clear, dry air loses heat at night; fog where cold currents chill the coast.

factCards.term: Climate change over space: five controls with an example of each
factCards.definition: Latitude (hot equatorial Amazon, cold poles); distance from the sea (Ireland's range about 10 °C, Verkhoyansk's over 60 °C); currents (cold Benguela: foggy Namib coast; North Atlantic Drift: mild Ireland); altitude (snow on Kilimanjaro near the equator); rain shadow (Western Ghats vs the Deccan).

factCards.term: Natural causes of climate change: five to name
factCards.definition: Milankovitch orbital cycles; changes in solar output; volcanic eruptions, whose sulphate aerosols reflect sunlight and cool the earth for a year or two; plate tectonics changing ocean currents; feedbacks such as ice–albedo and greenhouse gas release.

factCards.term: Volcanoes and climate: Tambora and Pinatubo
factCards.definition: Tambora, Indonesia, April 1815: 1816 became the year without a summer, with harvest failures across Europe and north-eastern North America. Mount Pinatubo, Philippines, June 1991: global temperature fell about 0.5 °C for about a year (1992).

factCards.term: How past climates are known: five sources of evidence
factCards.definition: Ice cores (air bubbles give past CO2, oxygen isotopes past temperature; EPICA Dome C covers about 800,000 years); ocean-floor sediments; tree rings; pollen in Irish bogs and lake muds; historical records such as harvest dates, frost fairs and ships' logs.

factCards.term: Ice Ages: the Quaternary glaciation and Last Glacial Maximum figures
factCards.definition: Began about 2.6 million years ago; glacial cycles of about 100,000 years over the last 800,000; we live in an interglacial. Last Glacial Maximum, about 20,000 years ago: ice over much of North America and northern Europe; sea level about 120 m lower.

factCards.term: Ice Ages in Ireland: the two cold stages and their evidence
factCards.definition: The Munsterian ice covered almost all of Ireland; the later Midlandian ice had gone by about 10,000 years ago. The evidence is drumlins, eskers, corries and U-shaped valleys; isostatic rebound and raised beaches are after-effects.

factCards.term: Milankovitch cycles: the three cycles and their periods
factCards.definition: Eccentricity (shape of the orbit), about 100,000 years; obliquity (tilt, between about 22° and 24.5°), about 41,000 years; precession (wobble of the axis), roughly 19,000–26,000 years. Calculated by the Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković.

factCards.term: Ice Ages: how a small orbital change becomes a glaciation
factCards.definition: Orbital cycles change where and when sunlight falls; when northern summers are cool, winter snow survives and ice sheets grow. More ice raises albedo, and colder oceans absorb more CO2 (about 180 ppm in glacials, 280 ppm in interglacials), cooling further.

factCards.term: Medieval Warm Period: dates and evidence
factCards.definition: Roughly AD 950–1250, mainly in the North Atlantic and Europe. Vines were grown further north in England than in the colder centuries that followed; Norse settlers led by Erik the Red settled Greenland from about AD 985, abandoning it in the 15th century as the climate cooled.

factCards.term: Little Ice Age: dates, three pieces of evidence and a possible cause
factCards.definition: Roughly the 14th to mid-19th century, coldest in the 17th. Evidence: Alpine glaciers advanced; frost fairs on the frozen Thames, the last in 1814; Ireland's Great Frost of 1739–40, then famine. Possible cause: the Maunder Minimum of few sunspots (about 1645–1715).

factCards.term: Global warming: evidence from CO2 and global temperature
factCards.definition: CO2 rose from about 280 ppm before the Industrial Revolution to over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s (Mauna Loa, since 1958); global temperature is up about 1.1–1.2 °C since the late 1800s; 2024 was the first year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial.

factCards.term: Global warming: evidence from ice, sea level and Ireland
factCards.definition: Arctic summer sea ice has shrunk about 13% per decade since satellite records began in 1979; glaciers are retreating; global sea level rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018; Ireland's average temperature is up about 0.9 °C since 1900.

factCards.term: Global warming: the mechanism and four feedbacks
factCards.definition: More CO2, methane and nitrous oxide absorb more outgoing long-wave radiation, so the heat budget is out of balance. Feedbacks: ice–albedo (why the Arctic warms fastest); water vapour; permafrost thaw releasing methane; less ocean CO2 uptake as water warms.

factCards.term: Global warming: effects on world climate patterns
factCards.definition: A more intense water cycle, with heavier downpours and worse droughts; more intense heatwaves (Europe 2003, about 70,000 extra deaths, estimated); climate belts and storm tracks shifting poleward; stronger tropical cyclones; sea-level rise.

factCards.term: Global warming: effects on Ireland and the scientific verdict
factCards.definition: Warmer temperatures; wetter winters and more flooding; summer drought risk, as in 2018; stronger storms and coastal erosion. The IPCC (2021) called human influence on warming unequivocal; the Paris Agreement (2015) aims for well below 2 °C, pursuing 1.5 °C.

factCards.term: Pacific in a normal year (Walker circulation): how it works
factCards.definition: Strong south-east trades push warm surface water west to a warm pool near Indonesia, where moist air rises (low pressure, heavy rain); the air returns east aloft and sinks over the cool east, keeping Peru dry; cold upwelling off Peru feeds the anchoveta.

factCards.term: El Niño: how it develops
factCards.definition: Every 2–7 years the trade winds weaken or reverse; warm water flows back east towards South America; the thermocline deepens and upwelling stops; the central and eastern Pacific warm well above normal and the rain zone shifts east.

factCards.term: El Niño: five effects around the world
factCards.definition: Floods in normally dry coastal Peru and Ecuador; collapse of the anchoveta catch and fishmeal industry, with seabird deaths; drought and forest fires in Indonesia and the Philippines; often a weaker Indian monsoon; fewer Atlantic hurricanes.

factCards.term: El Niño: five named events and what each did
factCards.definition: 1972–73, with overfishing, collapsed the Peruvian anchoveta fishery; 1997–98 brought floods to Peru and Ecuador and forest fires and haze in Indonesia; it, 1982–83 and 2015–16 were the three strongest; 2023–24 helped make 2023 and 2024 the warmest years.

factCards.term: La Niña: conditions, effects and a named event
factCards.definition: Stronger trades, a cooler eastern Pacific and stronger upwelling; heavier rain in Indonesia and Queensland, drought in Peru, more Atlantic hurricanes. The strong 2010–11 La Niña brought record floods to Queensland, including the Brisbane flood of January 2011.

questions.prompt: Describe and account for the characteristics of one global climate type that you have studied.
questions.model: Mediterranean climate. Location: the west sides of continents, such as the Mediterranean Basin, central and southern California, central Chile, the Cape Town area and south-western and southern Australia. Temperature: hot summers, with lowland July means of about 25 °C or more in southern Italy; mild winters, with coastal January means of about 9–12 °C; frost rare on the coasts; hotter summers and colder winters inland. Precipitation: moderate, under 600 mm a year on parts of the Puglia lowlands and Sicily, most of it falling from October to March as winter rain; summers dry, with drought for several months; winter rain often falls in intense downpours that cause flash floods and soil erosion. Pressure and winds: in summer the subtropical high moves poleward over the region, bringing sinking, warming air, clear skies and no rain; in winter the pressure belts shift towards the equator, so the westerlies and their depressions bring rain. The warm Mediterranean Sea also spawns its own winter depressions. On some coasts cold currents such as the California and Benguela currents keep summers cooler and drier. Local winds: the hot, dry, dusty sirocco from the Sahara; the cold mistral and bora. Vegetation: drought-tolerant olives, vines, cork oak and maquis scrub, with citrus where irrigated. Hazards: summer water shortage and wildfires in hot, dry, windy summers, such as the Mati wildfire near Athens in July 2018, which killed about 100 people.

questions.prompt: Describe and account for the characteristics of one global climate type that you have studied.
questions.model: Equatorial (tropical rainforest) climate. Location: close to the equator in the Amazon Basin, the Congo Basin and South-East Asia. Temperature: high all year, with monthly means of about 26–28 °C and an annual range of only about 2–3 °C; the daily range is larger than the annual range, with afternoon highs of about 30–32 °C and night lows of about 22–24 °C. The sun is always high and overhead at the equator at the equinoxes, and cloud cover stops temperatures rising much above the low 30s °C. Precipitation: over 2,000 mm a year, as at Manaus in Brazil with about 2,300 mm, falling in every month, with two wetter peaks after the equinoxes when the overhead sun and the ITCZ pass. The rain is convectional: intense heating and very moist air from warm seas and forest transpiration produce heavy afternoon thunderstorms. Pressure and winds: permanent low pressure in the equatorial trough, where the trade winds converge at the ITCZ; winds are light and variable. Humidity is often over 80%. Daily weather cycle: a clear, calm, humid morning, cumulus by late morning, torrential rain and thunder in the afternoon, clearing in the evening and humid nights. There are no temperate-style seasons. Vegetation: tropical rainforest on latosols. Human response: forest clearance for farming and timber.

questions.prompt: Climate characteristics change over time and space. Discuss.
questions.model: Space: climate changes with latitude, so temperatures fall and seasonal contrasts grow towards the poles. Continentality makes the annual range rise from about 10 °C in Ireland to over 60 °C at Verkhoyansk. West coasts with cold currents are drier and cooler than west coasts with warm currents such as the North Atlantic Drift, and altitude and rain shadows create sharp local contrasts; the Sahel is a transition zone that shifts with the ITCZ. Time: the Quaternary glaciation began about 2.6 million years ago, and over the last 800,000 years glacial cycles have lasted about 100,000 years. Milankovitch cycles change the distribution of sunlight by latitude and season, and feedbacks amplify the change: more ice raises albedo, and colder oceans absorb more CO2. Ice cores show CO2 near 180 ppm at glacial maxima and about 280 ppm in interglacials. At the Last Glacial Maximum about 20,000 years ago, sea level was about 120 m lower and Ireland was covered by ice. Shorter periods include the Medieval Warm Period and the Little Ice Age. El Niño is a natural shift that changes the Pacific: the trade winds weaken, warm water moves east, Peru gets floods, Indonesia gets drought, and the Peruvian anchoveta fishery can collapse, as in 1972–73. Twentieth-century and present global warming is driven by the enhanced greenhouse effect from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture. CO2 has risen from about 280 ppm to over 420 ppm, global average temperature is up about 1.1–1.2 °C, and Arctic summer sea ice has shrunk by about 13% per decade since 1979. Effects include heavier downpours, more intense heatwaves, a poleward shift of climate belts and rising sea level.

questions.prompt: Examine one distinctive global climate type with reference to temperature, precipitation and pressure belts (air circulation).
questions.model: Monsoon climate of India. Temperature: a hot season before the rains, with temperatures often over 40 °C on the northern plains; a wet south-west monsoon, from June to September, which is slightly cooler because of cloud and rain; and a cool dry season, with pleasant days and cool nights in the north. Precipitation: a seasonal reversal of winds brings most of India's annual rain, about three-quarters of it, in June to September. Relief rain falls on the Western Ghats and in the Khasi Hills, where Mawsynram and Cherrapunji are among the wettest places on earth. The Deccan lies in a rain shadow, and rainfall decreases towards the north-west, where the Thar Desert in Rajasthan is the driest region. Kolkata is wetter than Delhi. Pressure belts and air circulation: heating of the land creates low pressure over north-west India; the ITCZ moves north; the south-east trade winds cross the equator, are deflected by the Coriolis force into south-west winds and gather moisture over the sea; the subtropical jet stream moves north of the mountains, so the monsoon bursts suddenly. In winter the land cools, high pressure builds over the interior of Asia and dry north-east winds blow off the land, while the mountains to the north block cold air. The monsoon reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers India by mid-July. Late or weak monsoons bring drought and very heavy ones bring floods; the Odisha super cyclone of October 1999 killed about 10,000 people.
